questions.title: Benign tumours grow by expansion
questions.question: Benign tumours show:

explanations.A: Correct. Benign tumours grow by expansion: they enlarge as a cohesive mass that pushes aside, rather than invades, surrounding tissue. They do not spread to lymph nodes, recur after adequate removal, or grow at a rapid rate -- features instead associated with malignant tumours.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spread to lymph nodes is a feature of malignant, not benign, tumours.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Recurrence after adequate removal is a feature of malignant, not benign, tumours.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A rapid rate of growth is a feature of malignant, not benign, tumours.

questions.title: Malignant tumours grow by infiltration
questions.question: Malignat tumours characterized by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Malignant tumours characteristically show a rapid, not slow, rate of growth.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Malignant tumours are not localized; they invade and can spread beyond their site of origin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Malignant tumours characteristically do recur after removal, unlike a benign tumour.
explanations.D: Correct. Malignant tumours grow by infiltration: they invade and destroy surrounding tissue rather than merely pushing it aside. They characteristically show a rapid, not slow, rate of growth, are not localized, and do recur after removal -- the opposite growth pattern from a benign tumour's expansile growth.

questions.title: Tumour stage is the strongest prognostic factor
questions.question: The most important factor in prognosis of malignant tumours is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tumour grade (differentiation) informs prognosis but is not the single most important factor; it ranks below stage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Raw tumour size alone, without regard to nodal or metastatic spread, is not the single most important prognostic factor.
explanations.C: Correct. Among the factors that inform a malignant tumour's prognosis -- grade, size, stage and cell shape -- tumour stage, its anatomic extent of spread, captured by the TNM system's tumour size, nodal involvement and distant metastasis axes, is the single most important. A widely spread cancer carries a substantially worse prognosis regardless of how differentiated its cells appear.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cell shape alone, without regard to the extent of spread, is not the single most important prognostic factor.

questions.title: Invasion confirms malignancy
questions.question: A study is performed to analyze characteristics of malignant neoplasms in biopsy specimens. The biopsies were performed on patients who had rectal carcinoma. Of the following microscopic findings, which is most important feature to indicate that the neoplasm is malignant?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pleomorphism can also be seen in severe dysplasia without invasion, which by definition is not yet malignant, so it is not the most important confirmatory feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Necrosis can occur in a benign or non-invasive lesion outgrowing its blood supply, so it is not specific enough to confirm malignancy on its own.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An increased nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio can also be seen in severe dysplasia without invasion, so it is not the most important confirmatory feature.
explanations.D: Correct. Among pleomorphism, necrosis, an increased nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, invasion and atypia, invasion -- histological evidence that tumour cells have breached the basement membrane and infiltrated surrounding tissue -- is the most important feature confirming malignancy. The other four can each also be seen in severe dysplasia without invasion, which by definition is not yet malignant.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Atypia can also be seen in severe dysplasia without invasion, so it is not the most important confirmatory feature.
